# Discussion and conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

We set out to ask whether the standard remedies for class imbalance improve
prediction or only improve the metric. Our answer is that it depends on the
model, and that for the most common model, logistic regression, they mostly
improve the metric.

For logistic regression the remedies change the operating point, not the
ranking. Over-sampling, under-sampling, SMOTE and class weights all raised
sensitivity, often from below 0.1 to about 0.7 in the simulation and from 0.61
to about 0.90 on the credit card data. None of them improved ROC-AUC or
PR-AUC once there were a reasonable number of positives, and on the real data
they lowered PR-AUC by between 0.05 and 0.19. When the logistic model is
correct this is exactly what theory predicts, because rebalancing only shifts
the intercept and cannot change the order of the predictions. Our exploratory
look at the simulated data (@fig-simprob) explains why the remedies seem to
work at all: under strong imbalance even the true probabilities almost never
exceed 0.5, so the problem was the cutoff all along.

What the remedies do change is the probabilities. At 1% prevalence,
resampling and weights made the lasso's average predicted probability about
20 times too large. Moving the threshold reached the same sensitivity with the
original model, without refitting, and kept the probabilities honest. It also
makes the cost assumption explicit, since the chosen cutoff states how much
worse a missed positive is than a false alarm. This agrees with recent
simulation studies of risk prediction models
[@vandengoorbergh2022; @carriero2025], and for logistic models we think the
threshold should be the default remedy.

Flexible models are different, and there a remedy can genuinely improve
prediction. Rebalancing changes the trees themselves, not just an intercept.
Under-sampling raised the forest's ROC-AUC by about 0.05 at 1% prevalence in
the simulation, and on the real data SMOTE gave the best method of all, with
ROC-AUC 0.983 and PR-AUC 0.828. These gains depend on the measure, though.
In the simulation the same remedies lowered the forest's PR-AUC, and class
weights in `randomForest()` hurt in every setting. Part of the real-data gain
may also come from our own choice to grow each tree on 20,000 rows. This
fits the view of @elor2022 that balancing helps mainly when the classifier
on its own handles rare classes poorly.

The STAT 847 extension asked whether combining weak learners does better
than any single remedy. EasyEnsemble beat every single remedy on the forest's
ROC-AUC and balanced accuracy in 11 of the 12 imbalanced settings, with the
gain growing as positives became rarer. It did not help the lasso, and it did
not improve PR-AUC. Averaging helps a learner that is unstable, not one that
is already stable and correctly specified, which is the same lesson the
course drew for bagging.

Two broader lessons follow. First, a model should be judged on its ranking
before its cutoff is chosen. Accuracy is useless under imbalance and
sensitivity alone rewards any method that flags more cases, so we would
compare models by PR-AUC, with ROC-AUC alongside, and then choose the cutoff
from the real costs of a missed positive and a false alarm. Second, more
positives are worth more than rebalanced positives. Going from about 10 to
about 200 positives, from $n = 1{,}000$ to $n = 20{,}000$ at 1% prevalence,
improved every baseline at least as much as the best remedy did. Rebalancing
cannot create information that the data do not contain. An independent
second implementation of the whole study, written with different packages and
design choices, reached the same conclusions, which gives us confidence that
they do not depend on our particular code.

## Limitations and further work

Our simulated truth is a single logistic model with linear effects and
smoothly spread positives, which is the best case for logistic regression.
The real data show that the conclusions can change when the model is wrong,
so a natural next step is a non-linear or clustered truth, for example
positives generated in a few small clusters, to test our explanation of why
SMOTE helps the forest on real data. On the real data, each tree used only
20,000 rows, so the baseline forest saw about 35 frauds per tree; rerunning
the baseline with a stratified sample for each tree would show how much of the
forest's gain comes from resampling itself.

We also used only two classifiers and one rebalancing ratio. Boosting, which
is widely used for fraud [@leborgne2022], and partial rebalancing, which the
second implementation tried, would both be worth adding. The 10 real-data
splits share most of their data, so their standard errors are optimistic, and
the data cover only two days; a time-ordered split, as in the second
implementation, is closer to how a fraud model is actually used. Finally, we
measured calibration on only 5 replicates per setting, which is enough to show
how large the distortion is but not its full spread.

## Reproducibility

Everything in this report can be reproduced from the GitHub repository. The
seed is 447, set once in `R/00_setup.R`, and every replicate and method has
its own derived seed (@sec-simdata), so the results do not depend on the
order in which methods are run or on the number of cores. Rerunning stored
replicates reproduces their results exactly. The scripts in `analysis/` are
numbered in the order they should be run (Appendix @sec-app-code), and the
report itself only reads the saved results in `results/`; it never reruns the
simulation.
